faqs.q: What should I include on a Christmas light installation estimate?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business name, the client and job-site address, a dated line-item list (roofline lighting by the linear foot, wreaths, garland, timers, takedown, labor), a validity date, deposit terms, and a note that it is not a final invoice.

faqs.q: How much does Christmas light installation cost?
faqs.a: Most US companies charge $8–$12 per linear foot of roofline lighting with materials and labor included, so a 150 ft single-story roofline runs $1,350–$1,800 for the season. Wreaths and garland run $30–$60 per piece, timers $25–$50, and takedown is often bundled into the per-foot rate.

faqs.q: How much deposit should I collect?
faqs.a: 50% is the industry standard for holiday lighting — it covers the lights and materials you buy before install day. The balance is due once the display is up and the client has signed off.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate the deposit automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantities and rates, and the subtotal, 50% deposit and balance due update automatically.

faqs.q: Is this legal or tax advice?
faqs.a: No. Templates are for informational purposes only. Requirements vary by state — verify with your contractor board and a CPA or attorney before use.

deepDive.heading: Christmas light estimates: measure the roofline, then price the difficulty
deepDive.sub: The estimate is the document that decides whether the season is profitable, because it is where access difficulty either gets priced or gets absorbed.

blocks.h3: Measure the roofline first — it is the number the quote hangs on
paras: Walk the property and measure the eave run, then add the gables and any second-story sections separately. A single-story ranch of 100 linear feet and a two-story with three gables of the same 100 feet are not the same job, and the estimate should show why.

Per-foot pricing typically runs $3-$8 per linear foot installed. Access difficulty, pitch and roof material are what move a quote inside that range, so name them on the estimate rather than burying them in the total.
list: Linear feet of eave, gable and second-story roofline listed separately
Pitch and roof material noted — steep and metal roofs price higher
Tree and bush wrapping quoted per tree by height
Ground-level lighting and pathway runs quoted per fixture
Access notes: ladder placement, garden beds, slopes, and whether a lift is needed

blocks.h3: Quote the takedown in the estimate, not as an afterthought
paras: The single most common post-season dispute is a customer who assumed takedown was included. Quoting it in the estimate, with a date window, removes the argument before it exists.
It also changes how the customer reads the total. A season price that includes install and takedown is easier to accept than an install price that grows by $300 in January.
list: Takedown window stated as a calendar date range
Storage offer priced separately, since it is a recurring revenue line
Payment terms: deposit at booking, balance at install — booking deposits are standard in this trade because December capacity is finite
Season capacity note: the estimate can be declined if the install date passes
Whether the customer supplies any of the lighting, and at whose risk it is installed

paras: Homeowners buying holiday lighting are usually deciding between tiers, not between buying and not buying. Presenting a basic and an upgraded option in one estimate raises the average job value without extra sales effort.
Keep both options on the same page so the comparison is immediate — a second document rarely gets read.
list: Option A: roofline only, standard single-story access
Option B: roofline plus trees, wreaths and controller
Optional add-ons listed with prices rather than 'call for quote'
Both options show the takedown line so the comparison is like for like
Expiry date on the estimate, tied to remaining December capacity
